title: Jollof Rice
subtitle: West African party rice in smoky tomato sauce
excerpt: Long-grain rice cooked in a concentrated tomato, pepper, and onion sauce until each grain is deeply coloured and the bottom layer catches to a smoky crust. The great party dish of West Africa.

recipe.sourceNotes: Jollof rice is one of the most widely eaten dishes in West Africa, and the subject of a long-running friendly rivalry between Nigeria, Ghana, Senegal, and other nations as to who makes the best version. The name comes from the Wolof people of Senegal and Gambia. Each country has its own variations in spicing, the base sauce, and the type of rice used. The common thread is rice cooked in a deeply reduced tomato and pepper sauce, often with the prized smoky base known in Nigeria as 'party jollof' smoke, achieved by cooking the rice in a covered pot at low heat until the bottom layer catches on the pot.

recipeTools.notes: Heavy-based pan with a tight-fitting lid.

content.text: The tomato base needs to cook down until it is very concentrated and the oil separates: this takes at least 20 minutes and the mixture will look very dry and dark before the liquid is added. This is correct. The smoky bottom is deliberate: when the rice starts to catch at the very end of cooking, leave it for 2 to 3 more minutes. That char gives the dish its distinctive party flavour. Do not stir the rice during cooking or the layers will not form.
Blend the tinned tomatoes, red peppers, 1 onion, scotch bonnet, garlic, and ginger together until smooth.

Finely dice the second onion. Heat the oil in a large, heavy-based pan. Fry the diced onion for 8 minutes. Add the tomato puree and cook for 2 minutes. Add the blended tomato mixture. Season. Cook over medium heat, stirring frequently, for 20 to 25 minutes until very thick, dark, and the oil separates to the surface.

Add the stock, bay leaves, thyme, and paprika. Stir. Add the rinsed rice and stir to coat. The liquid should just cover the rice. Bring to a simmer, then cover tightly and reduce to the lowest heat. Cook for 25 to 30 minutes without lifting the lid.

After 25 minutes, check if the rice is cooked and the liquid absorbed. If you smell the base starting to catch, leave it for 2 to 3 more minutes to develop the smoky bottom, then remove from the heat. Fluff with a fork from the top, leaving the bottom crust in the pan. Serve with fried plantain or chicken.
